text:
#VOTE

The Price of Liberty, and the Eternal Duty of Democracy
Six hundred dollars may ease the burdens of a difficult day. It may bring comfort to a household, provide relief in a moment of uncertainty, or offer a brief measure of security. Yet there are treasures in the life of a nation whose worth can never be measured in dollars.
Among them, none is more sacred than liberty, and none more deserving of our devotion than democracy.
For money, once spent, may be earned again. Prosperity, once diminished, may be restored through perseverance and labor. But freedom, once surrendered, may demand the sacrifices of generations before it can be reclaimed.
History has taught us this solemn truth: the price of lost liberty is seldom paid in currency. It is paid in silenced voices, broken families, abandoned dreams, and the suffering of those who dare to stand against injustice.
The United States of America was founded upon a promise greater than material prosperity. It was founded upon the conviction that government derives its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, that human dignity must never bow before arbitrary power, and that the rights of the people are not privileges to be granted or withdrawn at the convenience of rulers.
Such principles are not merely the inheritance of the American people. They are a solemn responsibility entrusted to their care.
As one of the world's most influential democracies, America must aspire to lead not only through economic strength or military might, but through the moral authority of its example.
Let the world witness a nation where disagreement is met with dialogue, where political rivalry does not extinguish mutual respect, and where the peaceful transfer of power remains a sacred expression of the people's will.
Let no temporary reward persuade us to exchange enduring liberty for fleeting comfort.
Let no political victory become more important than the preservation of the institutions that make peaceful disagreement possible.
And let no generation forget that democracy is not a possession secured forever, but a living covenant requiring courage, vigilance, humility, and sacrifice.
To the people of America, and to all who cherish freedom across the world, let this be our enduring declaration:
We may differ in our beliefs, our circumstances, and our visions of tomorrow. Yet we remain united by a truth that transcends wealth, party, and power.
Six hundred dollars may improve a moment of our lives. But freedom gives meaning to the whole of our lives.
May America therefore remain worthy of its highest ideals, not by claiming perfection, but by demonstrating the courage to defend democracy, correct injustice, and honor the dignity of every human being.
For the greatest legacy we can leave to future generations is not the wealth we accumulate, but the freedom we faithfully preserve.
And may the light of democracy, entrusted to us by those who came before, never be extinguished in our hands.

text:
Think You're Priced In? Here's Why You're Probably Wrong

Many poker players believe that if the pot is laying the right price, they're automatically "priced in" to call.

That's one of the most common—and costly—mistakes in poker.

Good pot odds do not automatically make a call profitable. To make the right decision, you must compare the price you're being offered to the actual probability that your hand will improve or win.

In this video, we break down the difference between pot odds and hand odds, using real poker math, practical examples, and hand probabilities to show why the size of the pot is only one part of the decision.

In this video, you'll learn:
✅ What pot odds actually tell you
✅ Why hand odds matter just as much
✅ The mistake behind the phrase "I'm priced in"
✅ Why weak hands don't become profitable simply because the pot gets larger
✅ How to compare pot odds to your actual probability of success
✅ When a call is mathematically justified—and when it isn't

Whether you play live cash games, online poker, tournaments, or low-stakes Texas Hold'em, understanding the relationship between pot odds and hand probability is essential for making profitable decisions.

text:
The Tesla Roadster is mind-blowing. 
2028 release anticipated with reservations being taken now. 
Thank you @grok for the information. 

The Tesla shown yesterday (October 15, 2026) is the second-generation Roadster with SpaceX cold-gas thrusters. It is not a true sustained-flight flying car like an eVTOL, and the version that does the hops and flips is not generally available to the public. 
What was shown and the three versions
At a SpaceX facility in Texas, an uncrewed prototype used compressed-air thrusters (and a suction system) to drive upside-down on a ramp, flip mid-air, hop over other Teslas (including a Semi), and land. Tesla claims 0–60 mph in 0.81 seconds during the demo. 
There are three configurations:
•  Performance (“road ready”): Two seats, active aerodynamics + multi-mode suction system. No thrusters. This is the one open for regular reservations.
•  Thrust (“race ready”): Two seats + rear cold-gas thrusters for acceleration (claimed under 1 second to 60 mph). Limited release.
•  Rocket (“air ready”): Single-seat with ~10 thrusters around the body for upward, forward, and rotational movement. This is the one that does the flying stunts. Invite-only and explicitly not approved for public road use. 
All versions are claimed to have 300+ miles of range and top speeds over 230 mph. The thrusters use rechargeable compressed-air tanks (roughly 600 liters / ~250 kg of air in the demo car). Flight duration is short—hops and maneuvers, not long-distance flying.
When the public can have one
Musk said production starts in 2028. That is a target only (the original 2017 Roadster was promised for 2020 and repeatedly delayed). Reservations do not guarantee delivery timing or even that a specific car will be built. 
•  You can reserve the Performance now.
•  You can reserve the Thrust (higher deposit, limited).
•  The Rocket (the flying one) is invitation-only. Tesla has not published how to get on the list, and it is not offered for public-road use.
Cost
Tesla has not announced a final purchase price for any version.
Current reservation deposits (not the final price):
•  Performance: $50,000 ($5,000 now + $45,000 within 10 days).
•  Thrust: $250,000 ($5,000 now + $245,000 within 10 days).
•  Rocket: No public deposit amount (invite-only). 
Expectations in coverage are that the car will be expensive—likely well into the hundreds of thousands, possibly higher for thruster versions—but those are analyst guesses, not Tesla figures.

text:
A Wall Street Journal report and follow-up from The College Fix show that hundreds of U.S. colleges are using “direct admissions.” Schools review high school transcripts and send acceptance offers to students who never submitted an application. No essays, no test scores, no extracurricular questions required.

On the Common App alone, the number of participating institutions has more than tripled since 2023-24. University of Nevada-Reno’s admissions director told The College Fix the goal is clear: reach underrepresented students who might not think they can get into college and tell them they’re already qualified. He noted that most schools have DEI statements, yet the normal application process has little to do with those goals.

This is the workaround after affirmative action ended. Instead of students applying to colleges, colleges are applying to students—selectively, for diversity. Standards get bypassed in the name of equity. The result is the same old preference system under a new name.

text:
A publisher printed just one of their names.
In 1902, Under the Bamboo Tree, the song two Johnson brothers helped write in Jacksonville, sold over 400,000 copies of sheet music, all credited to a single name: Bob Cole. Forty-two years later, Judy Garland was still dancing to it in Meet Me in St. Louis.

The two names on that 1944 film credit were Bob Cole and J. Rosamond Johnson. Rosamond had written the melody in 1902, and by 1944 his name had made it back onto the page.

A third name had not. James Weldon Johnson, who had also had a hand in the lyric, was gone from the line by then.

Rosamond was used to his name behaving strangely on paper. It had started before the misprint, with the song that would outlast everything else he wrote.

His mother, Helen Louise Dillet, was the first Black female teacher in the state of Florida and gave him his first piano lessons at four years old. His father worked as headwaiter at Jacksonville's St. James Hotel, a job that put him in the same rooms as the city's wealthiest white winter visitors without ever letting him sit down among them.

Rosamond trained formally, at the New England Conservatory in Boston and later in London, a level of schooling few songwriters of any race had in 1900. Before New York, he toured briefly with Oriental America, the first Black show to play a legitimate Broadway house rather than a minstrel hall, then came home to Jacksonville and spent three years as Supervisor of Music for its public schools.

In February 1900, a group of men in Jacksonville planned a celebration for Lincoln's birthday. James, then principal of the segregated Stanton School, wanted a poem read at the ceremony. He decided a song would land harder, so he wrote the words at the family home and carried each finished stanza to his younger brother.

Rosamond sat at the piano and set them to music one verse at a time. James paced the front porch outside, working out the next stanza while his brother played.

Five hundred Black schoolchildren learned the result that spring and sang it at the ceremony. The brothers left for New York not long after and, by their own account, thought little more about it.

The children did not stop singing it. They carried it to new schools when they graduated. They taught it to their own students when they became teachers themselves.

Within two decades it was known across the South as the Negro National Hymn. The NAACP adopted it as its official song. It is sung today at graduations, at funerals, at the Super Bowl, printed in hymnals bound by churches that never heard of Jacksonville.

Every published edition of Lift Every Voice and Sing has credited Rosamond as its composer since 1900. The Library of Congress catalog lists him by name on the 1921 edition. As far as the record shows, it has never needed correcting.

James Weldon Johnson has a university professorship named for him at New York University, established in 2020. He has a body of poetry still taught in classrooms, a career as a U.S. consul in Latin America, a memoir, a place near the center of every standard account of the Harlem Renaissance.

He earned that record. Rosamond earned a melody, correctly credited on every copy, and comparatively little else carrying his name.

He kept working. With Cole and his brother, he wrote more than two hundred songs across seven years as the trio Cole and Johnson Brothers, several of them hits performed by white headliners who rarely said in public who had written their material.

In 1906 the trio staged The Shoo-Fly Regiment, a Broadway operetta about a Black soldier in the Spanish-American War, cast and built entirely by Black artists at a time when most stages offered Black performers only minstrel roles. Critics complained in print that the show was too polished, too "cultured," to read as authentically Black.

In May 1912, he performed as a pianist in A Concert of Negro Music at Carnegie Hall, one of the first times that hall had hosted a program built entirely around Black composers.

That same year, Oscar Hammerstein appointed him musical director of his Grand Opera House in London. It made him the first African American to hold that post at a major white theatrical company.

He met his future wife, Nora Floyd, in London that year and married her there.

Back in New York in 1914, he became the first director of the Music School Settlement for Colored People, training Black musicians who had few other doors open to them. That same year he joined the founding roster of ASCAP, one of a small number of Black members in an organization built specifically to make sure composers got paid for their work. It would be decades before another Black woman composer, Florence Price, joined its ranks.

When the United States entered the First World War, Rosamond was commissioned a second lieutenant in the 15th Regiment of the New York State National Guard, the unit that would later become the 369th Infantry, famous afterward as the Harlem Hellfighters. Before he shipped out, in 1917, he served as first deputy marshal of the NAACP's Negro Silent Protest Parade down Fifth Avenue, an event his brother helped organize, marching in near total silence to protest lynching and mob violence.

The march came a month after a white mob killed dozens of Black residents in East St. Louis, Illinois, and organizers wanted the country to see Black New Yorkers grieving in public rather than rioting in response.

In 1921, the Iroquois made Rosamond a sub-chief. It was an honor for how The Red Moon, his own Broadway show, had treated its Native characters, a courtesy few productions of the era bothered to extend to anyone.

Late in his career, Rosamond spent years compiling songs other people were letting disappear. With his brother, he edited The Book of American Negro Spirituals in 1925 and The Second Book of Negro Spirituals in 1926, adding his own piano arrangements to songs that had survived slavery by word of mouth alone, with no sheet music and no single credited author to argue over.

In 1937 he published Rolling Along in Song, his own chronological history of Black American music, complete with eighty-five of his own arrangements.

He was building an archive for a tradition, and a songwriting trio, that had mostly faded from popular memory by then.

In 1933, he wrote the score for The Emperor Jones, the film that made Paul Robeson the first Black leading man in mainstream American cinema. The credit read Music by Rosamond Johnson, Frank Tours. The score moved through four distinct movements, from African rhythm to a Gullah spiritual to Harlem jazz.

The film itself repeated a racial slur throughout, carried over from Eugene O'Neill's original play, and drew enough backlash across the segregated South that theaters pulled it within weeks. The controversy over the word swallowed most of what got written about the music.

Two years later, at sixty-two years old, Rosamond took the stage himself. He originated the role of Lawyer Frazier in the world premiere of Gershwin's Porgy and Bess, a supporting part in somebody else's opera. He sang it again sixteen years later, on the first studio recording.

By then he had written two hundred songs of his own, one of them sung by more people than almost any piece of American music in the twentieth century. He was still taking small parts in other men's shows to keep working.

He played his last stage role in 1940. He died at his home in Harlem on November 11, 1954, eighty-one years old.

He is buried at Mount Hope Cemetery in Hastings-on-Hudson, New York, next to his wife Nora. His daughter Mildred lived until 2007, long enough to watch the song become more famous than ever, and long enough to see most retellings of it still lead with her uncle's name.

The sheet music for Lift Every Voice and Sing is still correct. It has been correct for a hundred and twenty-six years, through every reprint, every hymnal, every arrangement for choir or brass band or solo voice.

What has not held up nearly as well is the rest of it.

The professorship that went to one brother and not the other.

The credit line that dropped a third of a songwriting trio from a hit forty-two years after they wrote it.

A materials scientist was offered $50,000 a month by a Chinese university, plus lab funding, and never disclosed the ties to the U.S. agencies funding his research.

That case is in a House Select Committee on China report released October 13, along with more than 700 pages of previously non-public NSF records covering roughly 30 researchers.

The committee says these are not paperwork errors. The files show repeated, multi-year patterns of hiding foreign appointments, Chinese compensation, and talent-program participation while taking American taxpayer money.

Enrique Lavernia had undisclosed positions at a Chinese university, joined China’s Thousand Talents program, and had about $5.2 million in federal awards tied to the case. NSF suspended him in 2020. He later joined Texas A&M and received a top faculty title in 2026.

In another case, an NSF program officer oversaw computer-science grants while secretly in a Chinese talent program and helped fund other researchers who also failed to disclose. He was later banned from federal funding. By then he was reportedly running an AI center at a Chinese university with military ties.

The committee wants the SIRA Act: clear government-wide rules that block federally funded research collaboration with entities on U.S. restricted lists linked to China’s military or intelligence work, plus stronger monitoring and real penalties.

Researchers collected the grants. They hid the foreign ties. Taxpayers paid for it.

text:
WHAT IF CANCER DOES NOT DEFEAT OUR IMMUNE SYSTEM?

WHAT IF IT SIMPLY EXHAUSTS THE VERY CELLS TRYING TO DESTROY IT?

AND WHAT IF WE COULD CHANGE THAT?

A fascinating discovery published October 15 2026 in Cancer Immunology Research may help us rethink one of the greatest challenges in cancer treatment!

Researchers at UCLA led by Dr Antoni Ribas with Justin Saco and colleagues identified a molecular pathway called CRL5!

This pathway helps regulate how proteins are processed inside cells!

But here is the remarkable discovery!

When researchers disrupted CRL5 in engineered cancer fighting T cells something extraordinary happened!

THE IMMUNE CELLS KEPT FIGHTING LONGER!

They maintained stronger tumor killing activity!

They showed fewer molecular signs of exhaustion!

And in experimental melanoma models they achieved better tumor control!

THINK ABOUT WHAT THIS MEANS!

We have spent decades searching for more powerful weapons against cancer!

Chemotherapy!

Targeted therapy!

Immunotherapy!

CAR T cells!

Yet perhaps we have overlooked a fundamental question!

WHAT IF THE PROBLEM IS NOT THAT OUR IMMUNE CELLS CANNOT KILL CANCER?

WHAT IF THEY SIMPLY CANNOT KEEP FIGHTING LONG ENOUGH?

As a practicing hematologist oncologist with an MD and PhD I find this distinction particularly meaningful!

In oncology we celebrate remarkable treatment responses!

But I have also witnessed the uncertainty that follows when patients ask whether their cancer will return!

A treatment that works today is not necessarily a treatment that will continue working tomorrow!

And that difference matters enormously to the person sitting across from us!

This is where molecular biology becomes deeply personal!

Why do some immune responses produce years of disease control while others fade?

Why can two patients with seemingly similar cancers experience dramatically different outcomes?

Could the endurance of their immune cells be as important as the genetic mutations driving their tumors?

The UCLA findings suggest that CRL5 may be one important piece of this puzzle!

And the implications extend beyond melanoma!

Imagine engineering CAR T cells to resist exhaustion before infusion!

Imagine combining these cells with checkpoint inhibitors!

Imagine identifying the molecular signatures that predict which immune cells will remain functional long enough to control cancer!

But important questions remain!

Could prolonged immune activation cause autoimmune toxicity?

Could cancer evolve new escape mechanisms?

Could we selectively modify immune cells without disrupting essential protein regulation elsewhere in the body?

These findings are preclinical and do not yet demonstrate improved survival in patients!

But they offer a compelling direction for future research!

And perhaps the most fascinating possibility is this!

PRECISION ONCOLOGY MAY NEED TO STUDY TWO SIDES OF THE SAME BATTLE!

THE GENETIC VULNERABILITIES OF THE CANCER!

AND THE MOLECULAR ENDURANCE OF THE IMMUNE SYSTEM!

Because the future of cancer treatment may not simply involve developing more powerful therapies!

It may involve helping our own immune cells remain effective for longer!

WHAT IF THE NEXT GREAT BREAKTHROUGH IN CANCER TREATMENT IS NOT TEACHING OUR IMMUNE SYSTEM HOW TO FIGHT?

BUT TEACHING IT HOW TO KEEP FIGHTING?

I would love to hear what fellow physicians and scientists think!

JC French IV “O” 204.5 Pass Yards
1 unit I -114 FanDuel

We’re targeting Cincinnati quarterback JC French IV over 204.5 passing yards, a number that offers an interesting opportunity as the Bearcats continue navigating Big 12 competition. French is a dual-threat quarterback who brings both mobility and efficiency to Cincinnati’s offense, but what I particularly like about this spot is the potential for increased passing volume against stronger conference opponents

With a line sitting just above 200 yards, we don’t need an explosive 300 yard performance. We need Cincinnati to give French enough opportunities to move the football through the air

Looking at his production this season, French has already demonstrated that he can comfortably surpass this number when the passing volume is there. Against Miami (OH), he completed 31 of 43 attempts for 309 yards and two touchdowns. Against Western Carolina, he threw for 245 yards on just 24 attempts while completing an impressive 87.5% of his passes. Those performances highlight two different ways French can clear this line: sustained passing volume or efficient production on fewer opportunities. His ability to generate yards without needing 40 attempts is an important part of the appeal

The Miami (OH) performance is particularly valuable when evaluating French’s ceiling. His 43 attempts and 309 passing yards demonstrated that Cincinnati is capable of shifting toward a more pass-heavy approach when the offense needs it. French completed more than 70% of his passes in that game, showing he can sustain drives through the air rather than relying exclusively on explosive plays. For a passing-yardage prop, that matters because consistent completions and extended possessions can accumulate yardage quickly

Another encouraging element is the way French responded against Arizona in his most recent recorded appearance. Although Cincinnati lost that matchup, French attempted 29 passes, a meaningful increase from the 13 attempts he recorded against Kansas State the previous week. His 153 passing yards didn’t reflect the same efficiency we saw earlier in the season, but the workload showed that Cincinnati can give him close to 30 opportunities against a conference opponent. If French combines that type of volume with improved efficiency, clearing 204.5 becomes a realistic outcome

French also brings experience from his time at Georgia Southern, where he developed as an efficient passer before transferring to Cincinnati. That experience gives the Bearcats a quarterback familiar with distributing the football, managing different offensive situations, and operating within a system that can incorporate both designed quarterback movement and traditional passing concepts. His mobility can help extend plays and create throwing opportunities when the initial reads aren’t available

The math behind this line is fairly straightforward. At 29 passing attempts, French would need approximately 7.1 yards per attempt to reach 205 passing yards. At 30 attempts, that requirement drops to 6.9 yards per attempt. Those are achievable efficiency marks for a quarterback who has already produced games averaging 7.2 and 10.2 yards per attempt this season. If Cincinnati establishes a consistent passing rhythm and avoids becoming overly dependent on its rushing attack, French has a reasonable path to clearing this number

text:
CLAIMS OF NONCITIZEN REGISTRATION OR VOTING: ANALYSIS AND TRACKER

Center for Election Innovation & Research (CEIR) - September 2026

One-Sentence Summary: A nationwide examination of noncitizen voting allegations finds that preliminary claims frequently collapse under investigation, actual instances of illegal voting are exceptionally rare, and misleading voter data can result in eligible American citizens being incorrectly identified as noncitizens.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

– Noncitizen voting is extraordinarily rare. Investigations consistently find only small numbers of potentially illegal registrations and even fewer votes.
– Initial allegations frequently overstate the problem. Many flagged records ultimately belong to eligible American citizens.
– The largest allegations amount to approximately 0.1% or less of a state's active registered voters, even before verification.
– Registration and voting are different. A questionable voter-registration record does not establish that someone actually voted.
– Government errors contribute to inaccurate allegations. Some noncitizens have been mistakenly registered by government agencies despite identifying themselves as ineligible.
– SAVE is not definitive proof of citizenship status. Its limitations create risks for naturalized Americans and other eligible voters.
– Corrections receive less publicity than accusations. Dramatic initial announcements often continue circulating after subsequent investigations substantially reduce their numbers.
– The evidence supports the effectiveness of existing election safeguards, while also demonstrating the importance of carefully investigating questionable records.

ARTICLE SUMMARY

The Center for Election Innovation & Research (CEIR) analyzed public allegations of noncitizen voter registration and voting across all 50 states and Washington, D.C. Its continually updated tracker draws on government statements, news coverage, and follow-up investigations. Its central finding is that large initial allegations routinely diminish under scrutiny, while confirmed cases of unlawful voting are extremely rare.

CEIR emphasizes a distinction often lost in political debate: a voter record flagged for uncertain citizenship is not proof of an ineligible registration, and registration is not proof that a ballot was cast. Mistaken data matches, outdated citizenship records, and registration errors by government agencies can all produce misleading figures. A newly naturalized citizen, for example, may still appear as a noncitizen in another agency's database.

CEIR reports that even the largest preliminary allegations represent no more than roughly 0.1% of a state's active registered voters. It cautions against comparing numbers across states because officials count different things and apply different standards of evidence.

The report offers several examples.

Iowa: Officials initially flagged 2,176 voter records in October 2024. Further review reduced that figure to 277 possible noncitizens, including 35 people suspected of having cast counted ballots in the 2024 election. By October 2026, the report says, at least six people had been charged in connection with the referrals: one convicted, four acquitted, and one awaiting retrial. These figures describe suspicions and legal outcomes, not 277 proven illegal voters.

Michigan: An extensive audit identified 16 apparent noncitizens who voted in the 2024 election, approximately 0.00028% of ballots cast. The cases were referred for possible prosecution.

Texas: A federal citizenship-checking system flagged 84 Denton County registrations. Local scrutiny identified some citizens and some people mistakenly registered by government offices. Fifty-six registrations were canceled after notices went unanswered, although reporting found at least one citizen among those affected.

CEIR scrutinizes the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system, which at least 28 states agreed to use for election-related checks. In April 2026, USCIS reported that only 0.03% of records checked required further review as possibly belonging to noncitizens.

The report says SAVE's incomplete data can misidentify eligible citizens. A lower court prohibited the expanded use of SAVE in June 2026, but the Supreme Court stayed that decision in September while litigation proceeds.

The researchers conclude that election safeguards generally identify the small number of questionable cases, while poorly contextualized preliminary announcements can exaggerate the scale of the problem.

CEIR recommends confirming citizenship through multiple reliable sources before removing voter registrations. Its tracker is broad but not exhaustive, and it records both substantiated findings and unverified claims rather than treating them as equivalent.

CITATION

"Claims of Noncitizen Registration or Voting: Analysis and Tracker." The Center for Election Innovation & Research, Sept. 2026, https://t.co/uG7up9xW5m. Accessed 16 Oct. 2026.

text:
Alberta would not be more prosperous separate from Canada. Separation means years of upheaval, a weaker negotiating position, higher debt, and no guaranteed access to the U.S. market Alberta already depends on. Becoming a U.S. state is even less realistic.

Even the Alberta government-commissioned University of Calgary study found that a smooth separation would leave Alberta's GDP 2.2% lower for the first five years. The supposed long-term gain is only 3.4% after more than 20 years, and it depends on favourable U.S. access, uninterrupted trade, energy expansion, and low borrowing costs all going right.

In the difficult scenario, GDP falls 16.2% over the long run, wages fall by almost $12,000 per person, and Alberta would need tax increases or spending cuts worth about $6,600 per person to close the fiscal gap. Replacing federal institutions would cost an estimated $50B to $170B over five years, pushing debt-to-GDP as high as 88.5%.

That is not a prosperity plan.

Separatists point to the roughly 3.5 million barrels a day Alberta sends to the United States. But most of that crude reaches the U.S. through pipelines crossing Saskatchewan, Manitoba, or British Columbia. Independence would turn Canada into a foreign country controlling the transit routes Alberta relies on, and the U of C report warns that Washington could use that as leverage to demand a larger share of pipeline revenues.

And "we could build a line to the border in three months" is not credible. Canada's regulator says projects with 75 km or more of new right-of-way take 10 to 20 months for assessment alone, before construction begins. TMX mostly followed an existing corridor, had federal backing, and still took more than a decade. Keystone XL had permits, Alberta money, and construction underway; it still died when Washington revoked its border permit.

Alberta's trade with the rest of Canada generates about $78B in annual income and supports roughly 334,000 jobs. Tombe's analysis estimates that a new border could raise trade costs by 5% to 8%, shrinking the economy by up to $62B annually. Separation puts access to both the U.S. and Canada at risk.

Some Republicans have floated Alberta statehood. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Alberta a "natural partner," and Rep. Andy Harris said the U.S. should make Alberta the 51st state if it seceded.

But wanting Alberta's oil is not the same as being able to admit Alberta as a state. Statehood requires congressional approval, and Alberta would likely send two Republican-leaning senators to Washington. Democrats would have little reason to approve that without a major concession, such as statehood for Washington, D.C., or Puerto Rico. No U.S. president can admit a state by executive order.

Trump's "51st state" rhetoric is leverage against Canada, not a serious offer with a legislative path.

So Alberta would not be choosing between Ottawa and a warm Republican welcome. It would be choosing between Canada and becoming a bargaining chip in America's partisan war.

Nor would Alberta automatically inherit American productivity by changing flags. Statehood does not erase geography, infrastructure gaps, or industry mix. And Alberta already leads the provinces in nominal GDP per capita and has the highest employment rate among them. It is not a poor region begging to join a richer country. It is already one of the most prosperous jurisdictions in North America.

Alberta has real grievances with Ottawa: equalization, Senate representation, regulatory delays, and federal energy policy. Those deserve reform.

But separation does not solve them. It replaces them with a new border, new debt, uncertain pipeline access, and a weaker hand in every negotiation that matters. And U.S. statehood is not a plan; it is a fantasy.

Alberta is better off staying in Canada, using its leverage to win a better deal, not gambling the province's prosperity on a separation it cannot control.

Marty O'Donnell spent two decades writing the music that defined a generation of video games — the haunting Gregorian chant score for 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐨, later the soundtrack for Destiny. Now he's the Republican on the ballot trying to flip Nevada's 3rd Congressional District, and President Trump wants him in Washington to do it.

O'Donnell first ran for this seat in 2024 and lost the primary. This time, he made Republicans an offer: he'd drop out if Trump backed someone else, so the party wouldn't waste resources on a needless primary fight. Trump backed him instead, posting it was his “𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵 𝘏𝘰𝘯𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘯𝘥𝘰𝘳𝘴𝘦 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢 𝘍𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘗𝘢𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘰𝘵, 𝘔𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘺 𝘖'𝘋𝘰𝘯𝘯𝘦𝘭𝘭.” O'Donnell 𝐰𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 in June, clearing the field for the November election.

His latest campaign stop: an old-school Halo LAN party in Las Vegas, turned into a fundraiser for gamers who grew up on his music. It's the kind of retail politics a career composer can pull off that a typical candidate can't.

His opponent is a different story. Rep. Susie Lee represents a district Trump carried by less than a point in 2024 — and this year, her own official account posted a profanity-laced rant about Trump attending Supreme Court arguments, writing “𝘴𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘺, 𝘐 𝘴𝘢𝘺 𝘧*** 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘥𝘢𝘺𝘴” before deleting it. Trump has since called her a “𝘙𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘓𝘦𝘧𝘵 𝘌𝘹𝘵𝘳𝘦𝘮𝘪𝘴𝘵.” on the campaign trail.

𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐝'𝐬 𝐋𝐀𝐍 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐮𝐬 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐬.

text:
Ailin Vilches Arguello, The Algemeiner
Israel is accelerating efforts to reshape its military for a new era of warfare, unveiling advanced technologies to counter hypersonic missiles and drones while planning a dedicated force to address increasingly sophisticated aerial threats.

In one of its latest advances in next-generation warfare, Israeli defense company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems unveiled a full-scale model of its Sky Sonic interceptor this week at the Association of the United States Army’s annual defense exhibition in Washington.

Designed to counter some of the world’s most challenging missile threats, the system offers a rare public glimpse of Israel’s push to develop advanced defenses as the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confronts growing challenges from low-flying drones, which have exposed vulnerabilities on battlefields in Gaza and Lebanon.

Traveling at more than five times the speed of sound, hypersonic missiles can maneuver midflight, making them far harder to detect, track, and intercept than conventional ballistic weapons.

Rafael first announced Sky Sonic in June 2023, but has revealed few details about the program, saying initial flight tests were expected soon without disclosing a deployment timeline or detailed performance specifications.

Israel’s latest defense innovations reflect a broader effort to prepare for future conflicts, as advances in missile technology, drone warfare, and other emerging weapons reshape the demands of modern combat.

At the same Washington exhibition, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) unveiled several systems targeting different threats, including a new counter-drone interceptor, a mobile radar platform, and an armed drone designed to deliver firepower from the air.

IAI’s HawkGuard system uses radar, electro-optical sensors, and artificial intelligence to guide interceptor drones toward hostile aerial targets and neutralize them through direct impact, without an explosive warhead.

text:
A STIGMA WITHIN A STIGMA: THE DOUBLE WALL OF SILENCE
It is two in the afternoon in a cramped Jomtien condo. A thirty-year-old woman is lying flat on her back on the mattress. The heavy blackout curtains are drawn tight. Her smartphone buzzes on the cheap nightstand—four missed calls from a friend at the bar. She doesn't call back. She doesn't cry. She just stares blankly at the water stains on the ceiling.

She hasn't slept properly in weeks. She hasn't eaten since yesterday. She hasn't shown up for her shift in three days. She messaged the mamasan to say she was sick, and she wasn't lying. She is profoundly sick, just not in the way the bar manager thinks.

She knows something is structurally wrong with her mind. She has known for at least two months. But she doesn't go to a doctor. She doesn't seek help, not because she wants to suffer, but because she knows exactly what they will say. Or worse, what they won't say, but will loudly think.

She picks up her phone, opens TikTok, and types the Thai word for "psychologist" into the search bar. She scrolls through the top three results, her face entirely expressionless. Then she closes the app, puts the phone face down on the mattress, and goes back to staring at the ceiling. The first barrier she hits is the professional stigma.

A 2026 study published in Frontiers in Sociology mapped out the brutal reality of this isolation. Among sex workers in Bangkok, only 20% had ever reached out to mental health support resources. A staggering low of 5% had ever contacted an NGO for help, and only 16% had ever reported experiencing violence to the police. The vast majority of the grid operates in absolute silence. This is not out of stubbornness or a lack of desire for help; it is driven by a profound, learned fear of the consequences.

The researchers noted that workers avoid mental health services "due to fear of stigma and a fundamental distrust of the system." That distrust is not paranoia. It is a highly accurate reading of a society that views them not as vulnerable patients requiring medical care, but as criminals requiring moral correction.

If the problem was solely the stigma of sex work, the solution would be relatively simple. A woman could just go to a private psychiatric clinic, pay cash, and lie about her profession. But she is trapped behind a second, much thicker wall.

In Thai culture, mental illness is stigmatized just as heavily as the sex industry itself. A 2024 sociological study confirmed that the reluctance to seek treatment is tied to "long-standing and deeply rooted stigma and discrimination regarding mental illness in Thai society."
The foundation of this stigma is built entirely on the Buddhist concept of karma. According to the research, Thais culturally tend to perceive people suffering from mental illness as individuals who committed bad deeds in past lives, and are therefore "receiving bad karma in their current life in the form of suffering from a mental illness."

This is not a casual metaphor. It is treated as a spiritual diagnosis. If you have severe depression, it means you deserve it. If you suffer from crippling anxiety, you are simply paying off a karmic debt. Going to a psychologist is a public admission that your soul is damaged. It is the ultimate loss of face. The societal default dictates that psychiatric patients are weak, and mental illness is a shameful family secret that must be hidden at all costs. It is a norm that enforces absolute silence.

Even if a woman manages to climb over both of those walls and actually books an appointment, she slams into a third barrier: the cultural incompetence of the medical system itself.

A 2023 study by the SWING Foundation revealed a critical failure point: "Mental health services are not culturally tailored." The psychologists, psychiatrists, and social workers in the public hospitals do not understand the mechanics of the neon grid. They do not understand the specific, grinding psychological toll of the bar life. They do not understand what it does to a human brain to manufacture fake affection and smile relentlessly for eight hours a night when you actually want to scream.
Medical professionals are simply not equipped to handle this specific demographic. They can write a prescription for antidepressants. They can offer generic cognitive behavioral therapy. But they cannot offer a genuinely safe space—a room where a woman does not feel like a tragic exhibit, where she isn't pitied, and where her survival strategies aren't judged.

A 2022 study published by Burapha University captured this bleak reality through the lived experiences of four industry women. One of the core themes that emerged from their interviews was devastatingly titled: "Psychological distress from sex work may (un)heal." The parentheses around the "un" are not a typo. They represent a deep, foundational doubt among the women that healing from this specific type of trauma is even mathematically possible.

So, what does she do instead? She does what everyone else on the grid does. She drinks.

The Burapha University study identified three primary coping mechanisms used by women in the industry. The first is utilizing alcohol as the primary assistant. The alcohol does not cure the depression; it just temporarily mutes the screaming in her head. It stops her from overthinking the reality of her environment just long enough to finish her shift. As one worker noted, alcohol helps manage the immediate psychological fallout because "it prevents you from thinking for a short time."

The second strategy is aggressive, weaponized hope. The researchers called it "hoping for hope fulfillment as the main driving force." She cannot afford the luxury of clinical despair. She has a strict financial quota to hit. She has a family in the provinces relying on her transfers. She has to build a house. If she loses hope, the entire economic structure of her family collapses.
The third strategy is the ultimate fantasy: the exit. 
"Exiting sex work is the exit from suffering." But quitting is rarely a viable immediate option. There is crushing debt. There are zero civilian jobs that pay enough to cover her obligations. She knows the exit is the only real cure, but she cannot afford the medicine. Not yet.
So she doesn't go to a clinic. She lies in a dark room with the curtains drawn. She ignores the ringing phone. She waits for something to change, even though she knows exactly how the grid works.

The SWING Foundation understands this paralysis better than anyone. In 2023, they conducted a comprehensive needs assessment among 200 sex workers. The data was a quiet scream for help: 58.5% explicitly stated they needed mental health counseling. 63% begged for worker-friendly services that wouldn't judge them. Half of them requested anonymous online self-assessments—a way to check their own sanity without leaving a paper trail, without giving a name, and without facing a moralistic doctor.

The numbers prove that they desperately want help. But they cannot access it because the system demands they step into the light to get it, and the light on the grid is incredibly dangerous. Organizations like SWING are trying to patch the holes, offering depression screenings using PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 forms right inside their clinics. But one NGO cannot rewrite the cultural DNA of an entire country. They can only offer a small lifeboat in a very dark ocean.

Back in the Jomtien condo, the sun finally sets. The room goes completely dark.

The woman slowly sits up on the edge of the mattress. She knows the bank account is draining. She knows her mother is waiting for the monthly transfer. She walks into the bathroom, turns on the harsh fluorescent light, and steps into the shower. She meticulously applies her heavy makeup. She puts on her dress. She walks out the door.

An hour later, she is walking down Soi Buakhao. The neon signs are buzzing. The baht buses are honking. She walks right past the entrance of the bar where she usually works. She doesn't look inside. She just keeps walking down the crowded street, moving through the noise, entirely alone, completely unsure of where she is actually going.

text:
Scientists have engineered a new class of self-renewing immune cells capable of fueling a continuous fight against both blood cancers and dense solid tumors. While modern immunotherapy has transformed cancer care, solid tumors remain remarkably difficult to treat because they build physical and chemical barriers that block standard immune treatments. Researchers have long hoped to overcome this using macrophages, the immune system’s heavy-duty scavenger cells that naturally push into dense tissues and engulf threats whole. Turning fully grown macrophages into medicine, however, has proven nearly impossible because mature cells refuse to multiply in the laboratory, resist genetic upgrades, and quickly get trapped in filtering organs like the liver and lungs after being infused into a patient.

A research team led by Qi-Long Ying at the University of Southern California, in collaboration with scientists at Stanford Medicine, bypassed this obstacle by looking earlier in the immune cell life cycle. Instead of struggling with fully grown macrophages, they targeted their immature parent cells, known as progenitors. By pinpointing a precise laboratory growth formula, the researchers discovered how to make these young parent cells multiply extensively in the lab while staying in their youthful, adaptable state. Because these young cells are easy to work with and can be frozen for long-term storage without losing their strength, they can be manufactured in large batches well in advance.

Infusing these immature parent cells transforms a short-lived treatment into a lasting internal defense system. Once inside the body, the cells travel straight to the bone marrow, settle in, and continuously generate fresh waves of mature macrophages and infection-fighting white blood cells. To aim this living factory directly at cancer, the team equipped the parent cells with synthetic tracking sensors that act like a molecular GPS, locking onto specific proteins found on tumor surfaces. They also built in a signaling feature that acts like an immune flare, recruiting the body’s own surrounding scavenger cells and killer T cells to join the assault.

In preclinical studies with mice, an infusion of these upgraded parent cells provided a steady supply of tumor-hunting macrophages that successfully suppressed both leukemia and solid breast tumors. Crucially, the treatment worked effectively even when the donor cells were not a genetic match to the recipient. Although human clinical trials are still required to ensure these self-renewing cells remain safe and controllable over the long term, the ability to mass-produce and freeze universal immune parent cells lays the foundation for off-the-shelf living medicines that could one day offer durable protection against hard-to-treat cancers and severe immune disorders.

Article Reference: Shi Yue, Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, et al., Qi-Long Ying. Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy. Cell, 2026; 189 (17): 5378 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.05.043

text:
Podcast: Sikh Siyasat discussion with Bhai Daljit Singh on the killing of anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota

Context
Parvinder Singh Jhota, a young activist who had been publicly confronting drug sales (including at local chemist shops) in his town, was killed, apparently on a live video. He had repeatedly said that if he were ever shot, his last words would be that drugs in Punjab are sold with government backing.
Both speakers treat his death as proof of what he was saying: the chemist involved had his licence cancelled multiple times and restored each time, and the attackers' boldness shows they expected state protection.

Core thesis: the drug trade is state policy, not a law-enforcement failure
Daljit Singh claims that after the militant movement was crushed in 1992, the K.P.S. Gill–O.P. Sharma police leadership summoned old smugglers who had gone quiet during the movement, supplied them drugs from police stations for about a year, and told them to push "every kind of drug." In parallel, a "cultural revival" program promoted vulgar songs and glorified alcohol ("eat, drink, this is life").
Host corroborates with: a 1993 article by UNI journalist Jaspal Singh Sidhu (no Punjab paper would print it) describing a liquor-soaked Gill-hosted press event in Delhi where a journalist praised Gill for turning "gun culture into jan culture"; and Gurdas Maan's "Apna Punjab hove, ghar di sharaab hove" at Thapar College as the branding of liquor into Punjabi identity.
The trade has since acquired more stakeholders: traders (highest profit margins of any business), politicians (drugs are needed to buy votes and retain followers), and gangsters. Daljit Singh alleges the gangster–narcotics nexus is run by the Home Ministry/IB.
Earlier individual anti-drug efforts (Khanna, Phagwara, Kharar) ended in killings; the nexus is too strong for lone individuals or single organisations.

Pattern: drugs as a weapon against rebellious populations
Wherever people have challenged the state — Punjab, Kashmir, the North-East — drugs flooded in after the armed struggle declined. A https://t.co/mMRchfFe3U reporter told the host in 2017 this is common to every post-insurgency region he has covered; Kashmir's recent surge, and Haryana's rise after the 2020 farmers' protest, fit the pattern.
The mechanism: break a people, then open the drug tap so the next generation forgets its history and blames itself.
Historical parallels: Opium Wars in China; indigenous peoples labelled "druggies"; a 1948 UN narcotics commission recommendation to list drugs as a tool of genocide, blocked by major states.

Counter-example: 1982–92
During the armed struggle drugs were almost absent, for two reasons: people were in a state of collective spirit, and militant leadership enforced a clear policy — traders or their patrons were fined or killed. International smugglers offered to move drugs alongside weapons, and liquor barons offered monthly payoffs; both were refused.

Structural argument: why no government will fix it
All parties (Congress, Akali, AAP, BJP) are "statist" parties that sustain Delhi's system; they share the same manifestos, economic model and materialism. Each campaigns on ending drugs (Amarinder's oath on Gutka Sahib, BJP's "drug-free Punjab") while the epidemic grows under each.
The modern capitalist state produces drug demand: profit, consumerism, extreme inequality, a majority left out who seek escape. States need the excluded to stay sedated, so they are never serious, only performative.
Cynical loop: the same forces that spread drugs return as NGOs, rehab centres and politicians offering "cure," blaming Punjabis.
Voters who sell votes for liquor or opium cannot be expected to fight drugs; outrage only triggers when something is caught live, then fades and the system re-normalises.
Resignations of the CM/DGP or arrests (e.g., Ashwani) change faces, not the structure.

Proposed way forward
Reject the parties; return to Sikh tradition of people power: sangat, jathas, Misl-style "hanne hanne patshahi," gurmata, panch pardhani.
Decentralised, autonomous local structures (a "polyhedral" organisation so suppressing one doesn't stop the rest), linked by a shared policy at the centre (as Akal Takht functioned during the Akali jathas). Inclusive of all Punjab residents, not just Sikhs.
Jhota's model is the template: guard your own area, on one issue, stay out of elections and side disputes. Long-term sustainability requires several local teams committing to that, not an emotional upsurge that fades.
Two obstacles the host flags: society's attraction to charismatic single leaders (whom the state kills, jails, buys or co-opts), and activists who contribute to central causes but won't build local structures.
Symptomatic responses lose a war of attrition against a "behemoth" state; the current era of global upheaval makes self-organisation, strategic thinking and capacity-building urgent.
Both note a Kisan Bhawan meeting (SKM, Dallewal, ~35 organisations) agreed the solution must be social, not governmental, but nobody yet has a method.

text:
What the video is actually claiming (and what it means for pDAI):

The video is a tightly edited presentation of research from the pDAI Research Group (Crypto Anon + NineIronCapital circle). 
It argues that a small set of “pioneer” wallets have taken effective control of the forked Arbitrum bridge and messaging infrastructure that lives on PulseChain.
The core claim is that this control turns a normally restrictive bridge into a custom gateway they can operate under their own rules. 
That, in their view, opens pathways to move or represent large amounts of value that can ultimately support pDAI.

The technical story:

On a normal Arbitrum-style setup, moving tokens from the L2 side back toward L1 requires corresponding assets locked in escrow. 
Validators (or their equivalents) propose a state root; after a challenge window it becomes accepted truth.
The video shows a specific contract (`0x1d60c6bc8afB07518b1112643ad1610c4732F19C`) whose functions look like L2-to-L1 messaging primitives (`l2ToL1Block`, `l2ToL1Sender`, `operator`, etc.). It then highlights a series of `changeProxyAdmin` / `changeAdmin` calls and an execution trace containing `isValidator`, `confirmTransferRoot`, `verifySender`, `messageSender`, `messageSourceChainId`, and especially `sendCrossDomainMessage`.

The interpretation offered is:

- The pioneers rewrote the permission settings on the relevant proxies and admin contracts.

- Because they control the validator/operator roles, they can approve their own state roots.

- With a customized gateway and empty local escrow, they can still fire cross-domain messages.

- This is presented as a structural bypass that could route toward the heavily funded real Arbitrum escrow on Ethereum mainnet (the video cites ~$1.8B) or, more practically, let them operate a private L2 environment where they mint large quantities of tokens and later move representations of them.

Supporting visuals include the wallet that deployed related contracts, its Ethereum-side activity (including a claimed $3M outflow in 24 hours plus ongoing inflows), and the single address that holds essentially 100% of the forked ARB supply on PulseChain (the enormous figure that matches known reverse-gateway style minting of the PulseChain ARB copy).

Closing signals: a July 15, 2026 message saying “L2 cross swaps soon,” the number 33, and timing notes that the message was roughly 90+ days old at the time of the video.

What this does  not  automatically mean:

Control of the PulseChain-side Arbitrum contracts and the ability to self-approve roots or call `sendCrossDomainMessage` does not, by itself, let someone freely drain the live Ethereum Arbitrum bridge. 
The real Arbitrum system on Ethereum only accepts messages and proofs that satisfy its rules and validators. 
A state root or message generated purely on the PulseChain copy does not automatically unlock real mainnet escrow unless the live system has been compromised or the actors possess legitimate credentials there. 
The more realistic reading of the research is that the pioneers can operate a controlled environment against the forked contracts - minting or representing assets on their side and using customized gateways, portals, or messaging to move value within the PulseChain ecosystem or toward destinations they control.

The video is advocacy-style research presentation. 
It selects and narrates the traces that support the strongest version of the story. 
More cautious public write-ups from the same research circle note that reverse-gateway minting and admin control are real for certain tokens and contracts, but many paths remain token-specific, conditional on destination acceptance, and limited by actual liquidity and source backing.

Implications for pDAI:

pDAI is the forked DAI. Its original MakerDAO-style peg mechanics (oracles, VAT, collateral system) did not survive the fork in usable form, so it has traded as a free-floating token at a deep discount for a long time.

The entire NineIron / pDAI Research Group thesis is that systematically capturing usable pieces of forked DeFi infrastructure (Aave portals, Compound, Curve pools, Across/UMA, Arbitrum gateways, Maker remnants, etc.) can create new ways to introduce collateral, liquidity, or demand that supports pDAI.

In that framing, the Arbitrum/L2 control matters for a few concrete reasons:

1. Minting and representation on a controlled L2:  

   If the pioneers can mint or issue large quantities of tokens (or representations of real assets) on their L2 side under rules they set, those can later be bridged, portaled, or swapped into forms that interact with PulseChain markets. 
The video’s talk of “trillions of everytoken” and then teleporting them for liquidations or capital is the bullish version of this idea.

2. Custom gateways and bypasses of empty escrow:

   Standard bridge paths are constrained when escrow is empty. A customized gateway plus self-approved roots is presented as a way to still move value. 
In the pDAI thesis this is useful if it lets collateral or stable-like assets reach PulseChain liquidity venues (Curve, Balancer, Aave wrappers, etc.) that can buy or support pDAI.

3. Existing reverse-gateway precedent:  

   The massive ARB supply sitting in one PulseChain address is real and comes from reverse-gateway style minting that has already happened. 
That proves certain destination-mint paths work on the forked infrastructure. The open question is whether similar or adjacent paths can be made to work for assets that are useful as pDAI collateral or demand.

4. Timing and coordination signals:  

   The July 15 “L2 cross swaps soon” message and the number 33 are treated as markers that the infrastructure was being prepared. 
Whether those signals were predictive or just narrative is secondary to the on-chain admin and contract activity that has been accumulating.

Practical take for investors who understand the fork:

This is not a claim that pDAI is about to be magically backed 1:1 by $1.8B of real Arbitrum assets tomorrow. 
It is a claim that a coordinated group has been accumulating operational control over pieces of forked cross-chain infrastructure and is trying to turn that control into a workable capital and issuance pathway for pDAI. 
The on-chain evidence of admin changes, proxy ownership transfers, and specific large mints (especially ARB) is consistent with that effort. 
The leap from those facts to “we can freely mint trillions and teleport them into real mainnet firepower” is the part that remains speculative and unproven at scale.

For pDAI specifically, success would look like new, usable collateral or liquidity flowing into markets that create sustained buy pressure or a credible mechanism that reduces the free-floating supply overhang. 
Failure or limited success would mean the captured infrastructure stays mostly internal to the PulseChain copies and does not generate meaningful external demand or collateral for pDAI. 
The research is detailed and ongoing; the video is the promotional summary of one slice of it. 
The economic outcome for pDAI still depends on whether those pathways can actually be funded, accepted by markets, and scaled - none of which is guaranteed by admin keys alone.

text:
The Monument to the Royal Stuarts is a memorial in St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City State. It commemorates the last three members of the Royal House of Stuart: James Francis Edward Stuart ("the Old Pretender", d. 1766), his elder son Charles Edward Stuart ("the Young Pretender" or "Bonnie Prince Charlie", d. 1788), and his younger son, Henry Benedict Stuart ("the Cardinal Duke of York", d. 1807). The Jacobites recognised these three as kings of England, Scotland and Ireland.

The marble monument is by Antonio Canova (1757–1822), the most celebrated Italian sculptor of his day. It was erected in 1819.

Description
The monument takes the form of a truncated obelisk. It carries bas relief profile portraits of the three exiled princes, and the following inscription:

IACOBO·III
IACOBI·II·MAGNAE·BRIT·REGIS·FILIO
KAROLO·EDVARDO
ET·HENRICO·DECANO·PATRVM·CARDINALIVM
IACOBI·III·FILIIS
REGIAE·STIRPIS·STVARDIAE·POSTREMIS
ANNO·M·DCCC·XIX
("To James III, son of King James II of Great Britain, to Charles Edward and to Henry, Dean of the Cardinal Fathers, sons of James III, the last of the Royal House of Stuart. 1819")
Below the inscription are two weeping angels, symbolising the lost hopes of the exiled Stuarts.

Other monuments
Opposite the monument to the Royal Stuarts in St. Peter's Basilica is a monument to Maria Clementina Sobieska, wife of James Francis Edward Stuart and mother of Charles Edward Stuart and Henry Benedict Stuart. Its inscription reads:

MARIA CLEMENTINA M. BRITANN.
FRANC. ET HIBERN. REGINA
("Maria Clementina, Queen of Great Britain, France and Ireland"[a])
Queen Christina of Sweden and Queen Charlotte of Cyprus, the only other monarchs with a memorial in the church, also lie entombed in the crypt below the basilica, with the Royal Stuarts. Queen Christina abdicated her throne in 1654 to convert to Catholicism while Queen Charlotte was illegally deposed in 1464 by her illegitimate half-brother.
https://t.co/ey7xKUvGRr

Sion's Powerful Rival: Frederick the Great,Templar King of Prussia and Head of High Masonry
According to Mackey's Encyclopedia of Freemasonry, "the exiled House of Stuart exercised an important part In the invention and extension of what has been called the High Masonry."21 We know that by 1755 the Templar Scottish Rite had advanced to 32 degrees. At the head of High Masonry was Frederick the Great (Frederick II), the powerful military leader of Prussia.
Mackey's Encyclopedia of Freemasonry tells us that Frederick "was initiated as a Freemason, at Brunswick, on the night of August 14, 1738, not quite two years before he ascended the throne."22
Frederick's initiation took place with haste following Ramsay's famous speech. Frederick had sensed that Templarism was being developed to topple the French throne. He wanted to use it to further Prussian supremacy. Upon ascending the throne in 1740, he became even more active in Freemasonry, initiating two of his brothers, a brother-in-law, and a duke into the Templar Rite.
That same year he called an urgent conference with Voltaire. Two remarkable events followed:
(1) additional degrees were added to Templar Freemasonry; and (2) instructions for a revived Order of Templarism were taken to Paris.
By 1746 Frederick's initiates had founded fourteen Masonic Lodges. That same year, after Radcliffe's death, Frederick became the acclaimed head of Continental Freemasonry. He then used the Scottish Rite for his own independent bid for the French throne, by trying to destroy the alliance between France and Austria. Time and again he created discord between Versailles and Vienna through his Masonic agents.
Sion was taken by complete surprise and forced to counter Frederick's political and military ventures. In 1750 Voltaire was deployed the second time to Prussia, to persuade the King to redirect his efforts toward the Catholic Church. Charles of Lorraine, the new Grand Master of Sion, took Austria's armies into several battles against the Templar king. Charles fought the monarch in a final battle in 1757 (called the Battle of Leuthen) and lost. Isaiah Miller recognized the woman in the stands. They had chatted for about 20 minutes at a game two weeks earlier. This time, the four-year-old climbed into her lap and rested his head on her shoulder.

His aunt, Star Balloon-Bradley, offered to take him back. The woman said he was no bother. She was happy to hold him, and Isaiah fell asleep in her arms.

The photograph was taken in Valdosta, Georgia, in 2018. After his aunt shared it, the family came to know the woman as Mrs. Angela. She had a teenage child of her own and told them she valued moments like this.

Isaiah’s mother, Thameka, later spoke to Good Morning America. Her son could be shy, she explained, but there were people he warmed to straight away. Mrs. Angela was one of them.

The picture traveled far beyond the game: a little boy with his arm around a woman’s neck, comfortable enough to sleep while she supported him. His family was nearby, and an almost-stranger had become someone he wanted to sit with again.

His mother saw something hopeful in the response, particularly amid racial tension. People were moved by a Black child and a white woman sharing affection so easily.

Isaiah had not arrived with a message for the internet. He had simply spotted his new friend and gone over to say hello.

Source: ABC News / Good Morning America, September 2018.

text:
The Unconstitutional-Law Factory

I have the right to, and the technical ability to, prevent enforcement of  unconstitutional speech laws, without breaking the law while I mass-producingly stand in their way of doing so. There are buttons we can push that can never be unpushed, like Bitcoin was created but can never be uncreated, it just goes on and on, and so do other inventions. Even if you kill the creator of bitcoin you cant kill bitcoin itself. We are declaring independence from unaccountable judges who grant themselves authority through precedent to hold as constitutional any law whatsoever, even if such law were, for example, to ban 100% of speech. This is the process that 100% of speech could be banned without violating the constitution, or so the majority of judges would say. And in response to this I build on tech that gov cant control, to prevent the enforcement of unconstitutional laws.

The Unconstitutional-Law Factory

Legislatures continuously pass new laws. Among them are laws that violate the Constitution.

A majority of judges hearing challenges to those laws can declare them constitutional. Higher courts can uphold those decisions, establishing precedents that subsequent judges continue to follow.

Even if 99.99% of Americans correctly recognize that a law is unconstitutional, that does not force the courts to invalidate it or prevent government officials from enforcing it.

If the courts continue upholding the law and government officials continue enforcing it, the restriction can remain in effect indefinitely.

The constitutional system has no mechanism guaranteeing that an unconstitutional law will eventually be struck down, even when 99.99% of the population correctly recognizes the violation.

Judicial agreement does not amend the Constitution. An unconstitutional law does not become constitutional merely because every court declares it constitutional.

The set of active judicial precedents has therefore created an unconstitutional-law factory and enforcement system, in which unconstitutional laws can become permanently enforceable, without any guarantee of correction.

Furthermore, we allege that powerful forces acting upon this system, including lobbying, blackmail, and other forms of corruption, have so thoroughly overwhelmed constitutional restraints in practice that the government increasingly behaves as though it has the authority to ban any speech whatsoever, provided it can offer a reason for doing so.

But the First Amendment does not say, "Congress shall make no law abridging freedom of speech, unless Congress or a court believes there is a good reason."

It says:

Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press.

If the government believes it has a sufficiently important reason to change a constitutional prohibition, the Constitution provides a procedure for doing exactly that: Article V, the amendment process.

The Constitution does not authorize lawmakers and judges to bypass that process by inventing exceptions whenever they believe an exception would be beneficial.

A sufficiently persuasive reason to amend the Constitution is not itself an amendment to the Constitution.

Therefore, we hereby declare invalid and reject, as a matter of constitutional principle, all precedents purporting to grant the judiciary collectively the unaccountable authority to hold unconstitutional laws as constitutional, without independent accountability to anyone outside the judiciary.

The Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Judges derive their authority from it. They cannot grant themselves powers that the Constitution does not give them, nor can their agreement with one another create those powers.

No number of judges agreeing to an unconstitutional interpretation can amend a single word of the Constitution.

text:
Happy Birthday Montgomery Clift

A four-time Academy Award nominee, Clift was one of the most sensitive and powerful actors to grace the screen. At his best, his performances were transcendent; simultaneously uplifting and tragic. Along with Marlon Brando and James Dean, Clift was considered a “method” film actor, but he was too inspired for gimmicks, and distanced himself from the term. Greater than Dean, and more expressive than Brando, Clift, with his haunting beauty, defies classification. Montgomery Clift was born in 1920, in Omaha, Nebraska. His first film role was opposite John Wayne in “Red River” (1946), directed by Howard Hawks, who saw a spark of something unique. Clift's second performance, in “The Search”, earned him his first Oscar nomination. Paramount offered him a contract, which he accepted on condition that he could turn down any script or director. Other studios professed shock that a novice actor could wield such power and there were rumblings about “the death knell of the producers and the moguls." Clift was on the cover of Life magazine by December 1948, and Look called him "the most promising star on the Hollywood horizon." His first film for Paramount was “The Heiress” (1949), with Ralph Richardson and Olivia de Havilland. The actor was unhappy with his performance and left the film’s premiere early. Actually, it was an excellent, nuanced piece of acting. In 1949, he shot “The Big Lift”, before playing the role of the ambitious but impoverished George Eastman in “A Place in the Sun” (1951). It was one of his greatest performances, and he spent a night in a prison cell to enable him to better portray the tragic young man convicted of murder. Clift was nominated for another Oscar. His perceived rival, Marlon Brando, was so moved by his acting that he voted for Clift to win, in the certainty that he would. Disgracefully, it went to Brando for his inferior performance in “On the Waterfront.” “A Place in the Sun” remains one of the greatest movies made about America. It also fostered an intense and briefly sexual relationship between the bisexual actor and co-star Elizabeth Taylor. Clift next made Hitchcock’s underrated “I Confess” and Fred Zinnemann's “From Here to Eternity”, which earned him his third Academy Award nomination for his perfectly judged performance as the boxer turned bugle-playing soldier, Robert E. Lee Prewitt. Again, he was unaccountably passed over for an Oscar. In May 1956, while filming “Raintree County”, Clift was involved in a serious car accident after leaving a party given by Elizabeth Taylor. Taylor found him under the shattered dashboard of his car, with his face bleeding and swollen. She pulled out some hanging teeth that were choking him before accompanying him to hospital. Despite reconstructive surgery, the actor’s face was visibly altered and robbed of its perfection. Clift returned to finish the film, and inspite of the studio's concerns about profits, correctly predicted it would do very well, if only because moviegoers would want to see the difference in his appearance. Unbearable pain from his injuries led him to alcohol and pills, and the second half of his 20-year career has been referred to as the "longest suicide in Hollywood history”. His next films were “The Young Lions” (1958), “Suddenly, Last Summer” (1959), and “Wild River”. Clift, whose health was deteriorating fast, switched to supporting roles in “The Misfits” (1961) and “Judgment at Nuremberg” (1961), in which he broke your heart. His increasingly erratic behaviour and substance abuse led to his being barred from film work. On July 22, 1966, Clift spent most of the day in his New York townhouse. His private nurse and companion, Lorenzo James, rose early and went to wake the actor, but found his door locked. James climbed up a ladder to enter through a second-floor window. Clift was dead. The official cause was a heart attack brought on by drugs and alcohol. He was only 45.

Senator Padilla claims the DOJ offered “no evidence” and no details. 

That’s false.

Completely false.

Federal agencies (USCIS + HSI) conducted a multi-stage data match of California’s voter rolls against immigration records, naturalization data, State Department records, and SSA data. 

The federal agencies involved used confidence-level matching, secondary review, and further investigation before identifying roughly 20,000 likely noncitizens who were mailed (or set to receive) ballots. 

The DOJ then provided California officials a specific list of those names on a password-protected drive and asked them to segregate the ballots pending verification—not cancel them.

California refused to even *review* the list. 

“No evidence” is just the talking point they use when they don’t like the evidence. 

But that talking point is demonstrably false. 

Noncitizen voting in federal elections is a federal crime. 

Demanding basic verification isn’t baseless—it’s the law.

text:
Have you ever wanted to wake up at night and pray Tahajjud but didn't know how to perform it?

Perhaps you're asking Allah for marriage, a job, children, forgiveness, or relief from a difficult situation.

Tahajjud is one of the beautiful voluntary prayers through which you can draw closer to Allah.

Here is how to perform it.

1️⃣ Know the Right Time for Tahajjud.

Tahajjud is performed at night, after ‘Ishā’, and traditionally refers to night prayer offered after sleeping.

The best time is the last third of the night, before Fajr begins.

The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah calls His servants to supplicate, ask, and seek forgiveness during the last third of the night. (Sahih al-Bukhari 1145)

Example: If Maghrib is at 6:30 PM and Fajr is at 5:30 AM, the last third begins around 1:50 AM.

You don't have to stay awake all night. Even waking up shortly before Fajr can give you time to pray.

text:
In 2009, Martti Malmi sold 5,050 Bitcoin for $5.02.

He later mined 55,000 BTC on his laptop and later sold most of them.

But the reason he got involved with Bitcoin is more interesting than the money he missed.

2009: a 20-year-old finds Bitcoin

- Martti Malmi was a computer science student in Finland when he discovered Bitcoin.
- He emailed Satoshi Nakamoto and offered to help.
- Satoshi accepted.
- Malmi worked on the website, documentation, forums, and Linux support.
- He also kept his node running when the Bitcoin network typically had just 3 to 5 peers online.

October 12, 2009: the first known Bitcoin-to-dollar trade

- Malmi sends 5,050 BTC to New Liberty Standard.
- In return, he receives $5.02 through PayPal.
- That's roughly $0.001 per Bitcoin.
- But he wasn't simply cashing out.
- He later explained that he made the sale to help New Liberty Standard launch the first Bitcoin trading service.
- Bitcoin needed a way for people to exchange it for ordinary money.

Someone had to get things started.

2009-2010: mining on a laptop

- Malmi kept mining.
- He says he accumulated more than 55,000 BTC.
- At times, his laptop produced 200 to 300 bitcoins a day.
- He joked that he only turned off the miner when he wanted to play Counter-Strike.

2011: real life catches up

- Bitcoin reaches roughly $15 to $30.
- Malmi sells more than 10,000 BTC to buy a studio apartment near Helsinki.
- For a 22-year-old who hadn't had much money, it was a big deal.
- Then he leaves his job.
- Finding another one takes longer than expected.
- He ends up selling most of his remaining bitcoins at prices as low as $3.

Years later, he looks back.

- Malmi has acknowledged that holding all those coins would have made him a billionaire.
- But he also says he doesn't feel he lost anything from the Bitcoin adventure.
He helped build the network, He met great people, He contributed to something he believed mattered.

Malmi's first sale helped someone launch a trading service.

His work helped more people use Bitcoin.

And his story became part of the history he helped create.

text:
Can condemning your country become a route to belonging?

On *Off the Fence*, Konstantin Kisin, Francis Foster, Winston Marshall and Tom Slater argue that anti-national politics can offer young people something positive even while it attacks the society around them: status, community and moral purpose.

Their reasoning is that education framed primarily around oppression can teach students to view their national inheritance as morally suspect. Social media then rewards public denunciation with attention and approval. For some young people, joining an anti-Western or anti-national cause becomes a way to demonstrate virtue and find peers who share a clear identity. The panel says this may help explain why white youths participate in protests that appear hostile to their own national culture.

They extend the argument beyond France. If national belonging is weakened while ethnic, religious and online identities remain available, social conflict may reorganise around those smaller loyalties. The panel calls this “Lebanonization,” a rhetorical description of fragmentation rather than a settled account of the events.

Their alternative is civic nationalism: a framework based on shared participation, history and obligations rather than blood or ethnic exclusivity. That framework would have to be genuinely inclusive, but also confident enough to ask newcomers and established citizens alike to join one public culture.

Does anti-national activism mainly reflect ideological teaching, or is it filling a real vacuum of belonging?

What do you make of this point?
